title: Λέαινα καὶ ἀλώπηξ
part: The Lioness and the Fox (Chambry 194 · Perry 257)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 194 (= Perry 257). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Λέαινα ὀνειδιζομένη ὑπὸ ἀλώπεκος ἐπὶ τῷ διὰ παντὸς ἕνα τίκτειν· « Ἕνα, ἔφη, ἀλλὰ λέοντα. »
sentences.tr: Leaina oneidizomenē hypo alōpekos epi tōi dia pantos hena tiktein· « Hena, ephē, alla leonta. »
sentences.l: A lioness, being reproached by a fox for always bearing one: « One, » she said, « but a lion. »
sentences.i: A lioness, reproached by a fox because she never bore more than one at a birth, said: « One — but a lion. »
sentences.n: ἐπὶ τῷ … τίκτειν is an articular infinitive after ἐπί with the dative, naming the ground of the reproach; διὰ παντός, "all through", is "always". The sentence has no main verb outside the quotation — the participle carries the whole setting and the ἔφη inside does the rest.

sentences.t: Ὅτι τὸ καλὸν οὐκ ἐν πλήθει δεῖ μετρεῖν, ἀλλὰ πρὸς ἀρετὴν ἀφορᾶν.
sentences.tr: Hoti to kalon ouk en plēthei dei metrein, alla pros aretēn aphoran.
sentences.l: That one must not measure what is fine by number, but look to excellence.
sentences.i: The story shows that one must not measure what is fine by number, but look to excellence.
sentences.n: A bare Ὅτι moral: the introducing verb is unexpressed in the Greek and is supplied in the idiomatic line. δεῖ governs both infinitives, μετρεῖν and ἀφορᾶν, with the negative attached only to the first. ἀρετή is excellence of a thing's own kind, what it is good at being — here, being a lion.
